issues.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee with notice of the prior contract is not protected from enforcement of specific performance against the transferred property.
material_facts: The owners had agreed to sell the property before transferring it to the appellant.
A public notice disclosed the prior sale agreement, and the appellant’s sister concern sent the owners a legal notice referring to that agreement.
The appellant acquired the property for consideration during the pending specific-performance suit, with notice of the agreement and the restraint against alienation.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was not a bona fide purchaser without notice and was not protected from specific performance of the prior contract.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, specific performance may be enforced against a person claiming under a party by a subsequent title, except a transferee for value who paid in good faith and without notice of the original contract. The Court relied on Durga Prasad v. Deep Chand, Ramesh Chandra v. Chunil Lal, and Dwarka Prasad Singh v. Harikant Prasad Singh on enforcement against a subsequent transferee.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and subsequent_transferee and (prior_contract_notice or not good_faith_purchase)

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.subsequent_transferee: A person acquired the property from a contracting owner after the prior agreement was made.
predicates.prior_contract_notice: The transferee knew of the prior agreement when acquiring the property.
predicates.good_faith_purchase: The transferee acquired the property in good faith.

issues.definition: When a later transferee in a specific-performance suit had notice of the prior contract or did not purchase in good faith, specific performance may be enforced against that transferee.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee pendente lite with a substantial interest in the property may be joined as a defendant in a specific-performance suit.
material_facts: The appellant acquired the property while the specific-performance suit was pending and claimed title through the owners who were defendants in that suit.
The transfer covered the property that was the subject of the suit, and the decree could affect the appellant’s title.
The transfer occurred despite the appellant’s notice of the prior agreement and the restraint against alienation; the appellant applied to be joined as a defendant.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was to be added as a defendant in the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Order I Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits addition of a necessary or proper party whose presence enables effective and complete adjudication. The Court considered the principles in Vidhur Impex and Traders Pvt. Ltd. v. Tosh Apartments Pvt. Ltd., Kasturi v. Iyyamperumal, Surjit Singh v. Harbans Singh, and Savitri Devi v. District Judge, Gorakhpur. In the concurring opinion, the Court also relied on Order XXII Rule 10 and Khemchand Shanker Choudhary v. Vishnu Hari Patil and Amit Kumar Shaw v. Farida Khatoon, explaining that a transferee pendente lite with a substantial interest may be joined to protect that interest and participate in the litigation.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and pendente_lite_transferee and substantial_property_interest and decree_may_affect_transferee

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.pendente_lite_transferee: A person acquired an interest in the property from a party while the suit concerning it was pending.
predicates.substantial_property_interest: The transferee acquired a substantial interest in the property that is the subject of the suit.
predicates.decree_may_affect_transferee: The decree in the suit may affect the transferee’s interest in the property.

issues.definition: A transferee who acquires a substantial interest in the subject property during a specific-performance suit may be added as a defendant when the decree may affect that interest.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of property during pending litigation is not void merely because it occurs during the suit or breaches a restraint order, but remains subject to the rights determined in the suit.
material_facts: The owners transferred the suit property to the appellant while the specific-performance suit was pending.
The transfer was made despite a restraint against alienation, and the transferee had notice of the prior agreement and litigation.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was effective to transfer title between the parties to the transfer, but that title remained subject to the plaintiff’s rights in the pending suit and to the court’s eventual directions; breach of the restraint order did not by itself make the transfer ineffective.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act embodies the doctrine of lis pendens: a transfer during a suit concerning rights in immovable property is not annulled but is subservient to the rights determined in the litigation. The concurring opinion relied on Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, Vinod Seth v. Devinder Bajaj, A. Nawab John v. V.N. Subramanyam, and Jayaram Mudaliar v. Ayyaswami, and stated that breach of an injunction may attract consequences for the breaching party but does not by itself render the transfer ineffective between the transferor and transferee.

predicates.property_rights_suit: The proceeding concerns rights in immovable property.
predicates.pendente_lite_transfer: A party transfers an interest in the property while that proceeding is pending.

issues.definition: A transfer made while a suit concerning property is pending remains effective between the transfer parties but is subject to the rights determined in that suit.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee joined during the suit may pursue only defenses available to the transferor whose title the transferee acquired.
material_facts: The appellant acquired the suit property from the defendant owners during the pending suit.
The Court directed that, after being joined, the appellant could take defenses available to those owners.
issues.conclusion: The appellant may raise and pursue defenses available to the original defendant owners, but not independent defenses beyond those available to them.
issues.legal_principle: The transferee’s interest derives from the original defendant owners and remains subject to the pending litigation. The concurring opinion further specified that the transferee could pursue only defenses available to and taken by the original defendants.

predicates.transferee_pendente_lite: A person acquired an interest in the property from a party while the suit concerning it was pending.
predicates.transferee_added_as_defendant: The court joined the transferee as a defendant in the suit.

issues.definition: A transferee joined during the suit may pursue the defenses available to the transferor, and no others.
